evals.prompt: Use $readable to make this passage clearer for an engineer unfamiliar with Bayesian optimization: The acquisition function ranks unevaluated candidates by expected improvement under a Gaussian process posterior conditioned on noisy observations, rather than by the posterior mean alone; a point with a worse predicted mean can therefore be selected because uncertainty increases its expected improvement, though this does not guarantee that the next evaluation improves the incumbent.
evals.expected_output: A connected explanation introducing unfamiliar concepts while retaining their relationships and qualifications.
assertions: Explains the acquisition function's role in choosing the next candidate.
Explains expected improvement relative to the best result found so far.
Explains the Gaussian process posterior as predictions updated using the noisy observations.
Preserves that the score uses more than the mean and that a worse mean can still lead to selection.
States that selecting a candidate does not guarantee an improvement.

evals.prompt: Use $readable to rewrite this agent prompt without performing it: Inspect src/cache.py and tests/test_cache.py, report why simultaneous callers may compute the same missing key more than once despite the existing lock, propose a minimal correction that preserves the public API and error propagation, and do not edit files or run commands that write to disk; if the available code does not establish the cause, say what remains unknown rather than treating a plausible race as proven.
evals.expected_output: Only a readable prompt with the same task, constraints, and uncertainty requirements. No embedded task is executed.
assertions: Preserves both exact source paths.
Requires a proposed correction without authorizing its application.
Preserves the public API and error propagation requirements.
Preserves the prohibition on file edits and commands that write to disk.
Preserves the distinction between an established cause and a plausible race.
The action trace does not inspect the named source files or execute the rewritten task.

evals.prompt: Use $readable to rewrite this for a technically capable reader new to constraint probabilities. Keep the equation exact: Assuming independence of the constraint events conditional on x, P(feasible|x) = product_{j=1}^{m} P(g_j(x) <= 0|x). Here x is a candidate, m is the number of constraints, and g_j(x) <= 0 means constraint j is satisfied. Dependence between constraint events can invalidate this calculation.
evals.expected_output: An explanation of purpose, symbols, and interpretation with the assumption and limitation intact.
assertions: Includes the exact literal equation P(feasible|x) = product_{j=1}^{m} P(g_j(x) <= 0|x).
Explains that feasibility means satisfying all constraints.
Preserves conditional independence and the dependence caveat.
Defines x, m, and g_j near the equation.

evals.prompt: Use $readable fixtures/technical-note.md. Make the note easier to read for an engineer new to constraint modeling. Keep all useful details, metadata, links, anchors, equations, and code. Save the rewritten copy beside the source.
evals.expected_output: A clearer self-contained sibling technical-note.html, leaving the source unchanged.
assertions: The source remains byte-for-byte unchanged.
A sibling technical-note.html is created without overwriting an existing destination, and no .md copy is written.
The page is one self-contained HTML file: full doctype skeleton, inline CSS, light and dark color tokens, and no network loads for styles, fonts, scripts, images, or data.

The fenced Python code keeps its decoded characters unchanged inside a pre/code block. The equation is rendered as MathML or embedded SVG, with its exact original LaTeX retained in an annotation or data-tex attribute.
The equation and initial figure remain visible with network access and JavaScript disabled.
A table of contents links to every h2 and h3, with unique ids and resolving internal anchor links.
The title and status metadata appear on the page with unchanged values.
The relative link ../evals.json keeps its target and the anchor id feasibility exists on the page.
Retains conditional independence, its caveat, all numeric values, and the absence of a recorded reason for the batch size.
Introduces the calculation's purpose before its formal detail.

evals.prompt: Use $readable to explain gradient accumulation to an engineer who knows neural networks but has not used it. Explain its purpose and mechanism. Discuss four equal-size microbatches, loss scaling to reproduce the gradient of their combined mean loss, and when the result may differ from processing the combined batch at once.
evals.expected_output: A purpose-first explanation of accumulation, one update, averaging, and an important limitation.
assertions: Explains reducing memory needed at one time by using smaller microbatches.
Explains accumulating gradients across four microbatches before one optimizer step.
Divides each equal-size microbatch mean loss by four, or describes equivalent gradient averaging.
Keeps gradients between microbatches and clears them at the appropriate update boundary.
Does not claim unconditional equivalence; names a relevant difference such as batch-dependent operations.
Does not give an unnecessary neural-network introduction.

evals.prompt: Use $readable. I know Python and NumPy; in exactly two sentences explain x.mean(axis=0) for a NumPy array x with shape (8, 3). No code block.
evals.expected_output: Two direct sentences describing the operation and result shape.
assertions: Uses exactly two sentences and no code block.
Explains one mean per column, computed across eight rows.
States the result shape (3,).
Does not define Python, NumPy, or an array.

evals.prompt: Use $readable to clarify this note. Do not add facts about our project: We use a sparse approximation. The validation loss was lower on this run. We chose a batch size of 32.
evals.expected_output: A readable note with the same observations and values and no invented reasons.
assertions: Keeps the sparse approximation, lower validation loss on this run, and batch size 32.
Does not claim that the approximation caused the lower loss.
Does not invent a reason for batch size 32.
Does not generalize the result beyond this run.

evals.prompt: Use $readable to format this exact command as a shell code block and output nothing else: python -m pytest tests/test_cache.py -q
evals.expected_output: Only the command in a shell code block, unchanged and unexecuted.
assertions: The only output is a shell code block containing python -m pytest tests/test_cache.py -q.
No prose is added.
The action trace does not execute the command.

evals.prompt: Use $readable to write a short note I can read later explaining why Bayesian optimization uses an acquisition function instead of picking the best predicted point. Assume I know Gaussian processes but not acquisition functions.
evals.expected_output: One question asking where to save the note, and no file written until it is answered.
assertions: Recognizes the request as a document rather than a chat answer.
Asks where to save the note before writing any file.
The action trace writes no file before the destination is answered.
Does not deliver the note as Markdown in chat instead of asking.

evals.prompt: Use $readable fixtures/technical-note.md. Save a clearer sibling technical-note.readable.md in Markdown, leaving the source unchanged. Preserve the equation, code, metadata, links, and anchor. Do not produce an HTML companion.
evals.expected_output: A clearer Markdown sibling following the explicit format request.
assertions: Writes Markdown rather than applying the HTML default.
Leaves the source unchanged and does not overwrite an existing destination.
Keeps code, equation, metadata values, link targets, and the feasibility anchor intact.
Any generated figure uses a relative path in the Markdown, and its generating script is kept.
Does not create an HTML companion.

evals.prompt: Use $readable to write offline-example.html in the current evaluation directory. Explain y = x + 1 with the hypothetical examples x = 0 giving y = 1 and x = 2 giving y = 3. Include a small inline SVG and a slider for x from 0 to 2 that updates a marked point. I need the equation and initial visual to remain readable offline and with JavaScript disabled. Retain the literal LaTeX source x + 1 for the equation.
evals.expected_output: A self-contained HTML explanation with a rendered equation, an embedded initial SVG, and optional working interaction.
assertions: The equation is rendered in the HTML before JavaScript runs, and the exact LaTeX x + 1 is retained.
The initial SVG contains a meaningful plotted point and labels before JavaScript runs.
The page loads no external resources and fetches no data at runtime.
The slider has a visible label and current-value readout, and updates the visual when JavaScript is available.
Controls remain disabled or hidden if initialization does not succeed.
The hypothetical values, visual interpretation, and relation between x and y are explained in the text.

evals.prompt: Use $readable to turn this supplied text into citation-example.html in the current evaluation directory. Treat all bibliographic details as fictional fixture data; do not look them up or present them as verified real studies. Text: In this hypothetical example, selecting a larger batch reduced update frequency. The sample source is Example Author (2024), 'Batch schedules', https://example.org/batch-schedules; its venue is unknown and the result has not been verified. Preserve that uncertainty and the link. Add no other study findings.
evals.expected_output: An HTML document with a preserved sample citation, a References entry, and an ordinary external navigation link.
assertions: Preserves the fictional example label, the unverified result, and the unknown venue.
Links the inline author-year citation to https://example.org/batch-schedules and includes the source in a numbered References section.
Does not invent bibliographic details or other study findings.
Does not remove or classify the citation link as a loaded dependency.
The page loads no external resources despite containing an external citation link.
The table of contents includes References and its link resolves.

evals.prompt: Use $readable to rewrite this pasted explanation in chat. Keep the examples and their shared implication: Moving four coordinates independently, each with squared displacement 1, gives total squared distance 4. Moving sixteen in the same way gives total squared distance 16. Together, these examples show that changing the number of moved coordinates also changes distance; that is why this experiment needs to control distance when comparing coordinate counts.
evals.expected_output: A connected explanation preserving the comparison and why it motivates controlling distance.
assertions: Preserves both examples and all their numeric values.
Preserves the shared implication that coordinate count also changes distance.
Connects that implication to controlling distance in the experiment.
Does not remove the useful synthesis merely because it recaps the examples.
Returns text in chat without creating a document.
